opus-5.5.text:
I'd say it's surprising in some ways and less surprising in others. What's less surprising is that these models learn meaningful biology at all. Protein language models are trained on hundreds of millions of sequences, and evolution has already done an enormous amount of experimentation for us. If a motif is functionally important, it's going to show up again and again across families, so a model trying to predict masked residues has every incentive to pick up on those patterns. In that sense, we'd almost expect the model to have internalized a lot of structural and functional regularities.

What was genuinely surprising to me is how much of that knowledge turns out to be legible once you use the right interpretability tools. When we apply things like sparse autoencoders to the internal representations, a lot of the features line up quite cleanly with concepts biologists already know, like binding sites, certain secondary structure elements, and known domains. That's a nice sanity check. But then you find features that are clearly consistent and clearly activating on specific patterns, and they don't map onto any existing annotation. Those are the exciting ones, because they point to motifs that may have been sitting in the data all along without anyone giving them a name.

I'd add a caveat, though. A feature in a model isn't a biological discovery by itself. It's a hypothesis. Sometimes it reflects a real functional or structural unit, and sometimes it reflects a quirk of the training data, like sequence redundancy or how certain families are overrepresented in the databases. So the critical step is going back to the bench, or at least to structural data and independent datasets, to check whether the motif does something.

The bigger shift, I think, is conceptual. We've usually treated these models as black-box predictors: give it a sequence, get a structure or a fitness score. Interpretability turns the model into something closer to a scientific instrument, almost like a microscope pointed at the patterns evolution has left behind. The fact that you can extract new candidate biology that way, rather than only better predictions, is what I find most surprising and most promising.

r001.rationale: It says motifs may have been present in the data without an existing annotation, but does not identify limitations in annotation databases as a reason to expect models to learn them.

r002.rationale: It does not comment on how frequently new protein motifs are reported in the scientific literature.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I'd say I was surprised, but in a way that I think is instructive about where this field is going.

Going into it, our expectation was fairly modest. We trained sparse autoencoders on the internal activations of ESM-2, and the hope was that we'd recover things we already knew — that there would be features corresponding to, say, zinc fingers or transmembrane helices or known binding sites, and that this would serve as a kind of sanity check that the model had learned something biologically meaningful rather than just statistical regularities of amino acid sequences. And we did find that. A large fraction of the features map cleanly onto annotations in databases like InterPro or Swiss-Prot, which was reassuring.

What surprised me was the other part. There was a substantial set of features that were clearly structured — they fired consistently on specific sequence patterns across many unrelated proteins, often with a clear spatial logic when you mapped them onto structures — but they didn't correspond to anything in the existing annotation databases. And when we dug into some of those, they looked like genuine biological motifs that just hadn't been catalogued. Some of them we could partially rationalize after the fact, which in a sense is the ideal outcome: the model points at something, and then a human biologist can look at it and say, oh, that actually makes sense given what we know about this family of enzymes.

So the surprise, for me, wasn't really that a model trained on hundreds of millions of sequences had picked up on patterns humans hadn't written down. In retrospect that seems almost inevitable — the model has seen far more sequence data than any individual researcher, and it's under pressure to compress that data efficiently. The surprise was that interpretability tools were mature enough to actually extract those patterns in a form a biologist could act on. A few years ago, I would have said the model probably "knows" things we don't, but that we have no realistic way of reading them out. The sparse autoencoder approach changed that.

I'd also add a note of caution, because I think it's easy to overstate this. Not every unannotated feature is a discovery. Some of them are artifacts of the training data — bias toward certain organisms, sequencing errors, redundancy in the databases. So the right framing is that the model generates hypotheses at scale, and some fraction of those hypotheses turn out to be real biology. That's still extremely valuable, because hypothesis generation is often the bottleneck. But it means the human in the loop doesn't go away. If anything, the job of the biologist shifts toward triaging and validating what the model surfaces.

The broader thing I take from it is that interpretability is not just a safety or trust tool. It can be a scientific instrument. We've spent a lot of time asking whether we can trust what these models do. This flips it around and asks what they can teach us. And I suspect proteins are just the first domain where that becomes practical.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s quite surprising and exciting, especially because these models are trained on protein sequences rather than explicitly taught the biological meaning of different motifs. Their training objective is essentially to predict missing amino acids, but doing that well seems to require learning some of the underlying structure and biology of proteins.

So when we interpret the model, we can ask: Has it learned patterns that correspond to motifs we already know? And then, more interestingly, are there patterns it consistently recognizes that we haven’t characterized yet?

The important distinction is that finding a pattern in the model doesn’t automatically establish a new biological discovery. It gives us a hypothesis that we can then test experimentally. That’s what excites me: interpretability can become a tool for generating scientific hypotheses, in addition to helping us understand how the model works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s surprising, but in a way that makes sense once you think about what these models are learning. A protein language model is trained on sequences, without us explicitly telling it which motifs to look for. But to capture the patterns in those sequences, it has to learn something about the constraints that govern proteins—their structure and their function.

The exciting question is whether we can turn those learned patterns into something we can understand. If we identify a feature that corresponds to a known motif, that gives us some confidence that the model is capturing meaningful biology. Then we can look at features that don’t correspond to an existing annotation and ask whether they suggest something new.

Of course, an unfamiliar pattern isn’t automatically a new biological discovery. You still need to validate it. But it makes interpretation potentially much more powerful: it can help us generate hypotheses about biology, in addition to explaining a model’s predictions.
